details:
NASA FIRE NIA — Spatial Fire Activity Analysis

NASA FIRE NIA is an analytical project focused on improving the understanding of active fire patterns through the spatial analysis of satellite observations.

The project addresses the challenge of harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS active fire hotspot information to support a more consistent understanding of fire activity across different satellite observation sources.

The VE88–VE91 analytical work processes six VIIRS observations, identified as V0175 through V0180, and examines their geographic relationships using distance calculations and spatial clustering.

Three geographic clusters were identified using a 10 km clustering threshold:

  • Cluster 1: V0175, V0176, V0177.
  • Cluster 2: V0178.
  • Cluster 3: V0179, V0180.

The analysis includes geographic cluster centers, cluster compactness, cluster separation, VIIRS-to-MODIS distance comparisons, and Fire Radiative Power (FRP) distribution.

The total recorded VIIRS FRP is 69.70. Cluster-level analysis identifies differences in fire radiative power and spatial concentration.

Cluster stability was examined across five distance thresholds: 5 km, 10 km, 15 km, 20 km, and 40 km. The original 10 km clustering partition was successfully reproduced.

An independent reconciliation recalculated all 15 VIIRS-to-VIIRS pair distances. No distance mismatches or connectivity mismatches were identified.

The project preserves its historical architecture evidence as a separate branch from the spatial analytical results. Historical RC-02 through RC-05 evidence is maintained unchanged and is not presented as spatial-analysis testing.

NASA FIRE NIA provides a structured analytical foundation for examining satellite-detected fire patterns, spatial relationships, clustering behavior, and FRP distribution.

The results demonstrate how organized satellite observation data can support further development of fire monitoring, historical analysis, and early-warning applications.

The current submission documents the verified analytical work and its limitations. It does not claim that a complete operational fire-warning system has already been deployed.
